Prefix reuse patterns and prompt normalization

transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: All right, welcome everyone. Um this is the Cedar pilot weekly sync, thanks for carving time. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Alex Romero: Alex here, ML lead.
[00:15] Priya Shah: Priya, platform.
[00:17] Mark Li: Mark, CTO.
[00:19] Elena Gomez: Elena from security.
[00:21] Jordan Park: Great, and Maya is with me from solutions. Maya?
[00:25] Maya Singh: Hi all, hey.
[00:28] Jordan Park: Cool. Agenda — quick data recap, we saw a hit-rate dip last Thursday after the synthetic load test, go over root cause hypotheses, tuning recommendations (eviction, prefetch, batching), then security questions and next steps. Sound good?
[00:42] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Also want to confirm timeline for pilot ramp — are we still aiming for stage gate by mid-July?
[00:50] Jordan Park: Yes we are, mid-July for stage gate. We'll need the sample prompt set this week to finalize success criteria.
[00:56] Alex Romero: Quick note — the drop was pretty sharp. We went from 72% KV hit to 44% at peak churn.
[01:05] Maya Singh: Right. Thanks Alex. We pulled the logs and saw two things: first prefix normalization mismatch, like some of your client sessions append timestamps and dynamic tokens, so the cache keys don't align. Second, eviction storms from a set of new ephemeral sessions.
[01:26] Alex Romero: Yeah the clients do include a user-id hash and sometimes a session nonce in the prompt metadata. We thought it was removed server-side but apparently not always.
[01:34] Jordan Park: Ok so hypothesis A — key fragmentation from prompt variability. Hypothesis B — sudden user churn created cohort churn that overflowed KV working set causing evictions. Hypothesis C — our prefetch heuristics didn't trigger because sequence signatures didn't match expected patterns.
[01:50] Mark Li: Can you explain what you mean by prefetch heuristics? I thought we only relied on LRU.
[01:57] Maya Singh: Sure — Redwood has a lightweight prefetch that looks at session-level patterns; if we see recurring prefixes in the session it pre-warms the KV cache for subsequent tokens. But it needs consistent prefix signatures. If the prefix is noisy we won't prefetch.
[02:12] Elena Gomez: From a compliance POV I need to understand what logs you store and how long. The pilot team noticed raw prompt snippets in logs previously.
[02:21] Jordan Park: Good call. For the pilot we've been retaining request metadata and KV lookup keys for 30 days, and full prompts were masked in transit, but I'll confirm exact fields. We'll also propose a strict log redaction plan for the dedicated deployment.
[02:36] Priya Shah: On normalization — we can likely remove nonce at client if recommended, but we need a backward-compatible approach.
[02:44] Alex Romero: Agreed — we can ship a client-side normalization step to strip volatile fields but can't break older clients immediately.
[02:51] Maya Singh: One strategy — server-side canonicalization layer that maps variants to canonical prefix keys. Adds a tiny CPU cost but avoids client changes.
[02:59] Jordan Park: Let's walk through the numbers quickly. Maya, can you run us through the hit-rate timeline and latency impact?
[03:06] Maya Singh: Yeah. Uploaded chart link in the chat (drive/cedar/pilot/hitrate-2026-06-29.png). Baseline week before test: KV hit 72%, prefix reuse 38%, average p50 token latency 46ms. After synthetic spike: KV hit 44%, prefix reuse down to 19%, p50 token latency jumped to 78ms; p95 token latency impacted more — saw tail at ~310ms during eviction storms.
[03:34] Alex Romero: Oof. That p95 hitting 300ms is concerning for our UI.
[03:38] Jordan Park: Yes. So recommended mitigations: 1) prompt normalization/canonicalization to reduce key fragmentation; 2) adjust eviction policy to be cohort-aware (protect long-lived sessions); 3) tune prefetch threshold to be more aggressive for recognized prefixes; 4) temporary increase reserved capacity to smooth the churn.
[03:58] Mark Li: Can you quantify the cost of temporary reserved capacity? We need to weigh that against engineering time.
[04:05] Jordan Park: We'll send a cost projection. Rough ballpark: a small reserved bucket for two days was estimated at ~$1.2k based on current usage — Maya, is that right?
[04:14] Maya Singh: Ballpark yes, but I'll produce a tuned sheet with batching gains folded in. Bigger lever is batching — increasing batch depth for certain low-latency routes can reduce per-token cost by ~18% in our sim.
[04:27] Priya Shah: Batching will increase p50 slightly, right? We can't blow up our p95.
[04:31] Maya Singh: Correct — batching introduces micro-queueing. With our recommended config (adaptive batching with p50 target of 60ms) we kept p95 within acceptable range in tests — I'll share numbers.
[04:43] Alex Romero: On eviction policy: what does cohort-aware mean concretely?
[04:47] Maya Singh: We group keys by session fingerprint and maintain a small protected quota for stable sessions — keys that show repeated reuse in a time window get lower eviction priority. This keeps hot long-lived prefixes alive despite churn. It's a hybrid of LRU + frequency.
[05:00] Mark Li: Sounds promising. Any risk of cache bloat?
[05:03] Maya Singh: If misconfigured, yes. But in our sim we set protected quota to 20% of working set and saw hit-rate uplift without exceeding memory.
[05:12] Elena Gomez: Regarding logs and KMS — we need to see proposed retention and key rotation cadence. We also need proof of SOC/ISO posture for a private deployment.
[05:21] Jordan Park: We'll attach our compliance pack. For keys we support KMS integrations with rotation policies; we'll document how logs are redacted before landing in S3.
[05:29] Priya Shah: Ok on canonicalization — could there be false positives where two distinct prompts map to the same canonical key? That could affect quality.
[05:38] Maya Singh: That's the tradeoff. Our canonicalization is conservative — removes known volatile fields and normalizes whitespace and casing; we also keep a hashed sidecar of full prompt to validate during A/B checks. If collisions cause quality drift we can roll back quickly.
[05:52] Alex Romero: Can we do an experiment: run canonicalization in shadow mode (i.e., compute canonical keys but not use them for cache reads), then compare hit-rate and collision estimate?
[06:01] Maya Singh: Yes absolutely. That's low risk and will give us collision signal. We'll run that during the eviction sim.
[06:08] Jordan Park: Great. Action item for Maya: run 24h eviction simulation with two variants — baseline, and baseline+shadow-canonicalization — and produce hit-rate and collision estimates.
[06:18] Maya Singh: Noted.
[06:20] Mark Li: On instrumentation: can you export per-prefix reuse histograms? We need to see heavy hitters so product can tweak templates.
[06:28] Maya Singh: Yes we already have per-prefix histograms in the dashboard. I'll generate a top-200 prefix report and send a CSV link.
[06:35] Alex Romero: We'll also flag client code that appends dynamic telemetry into the prompt. We can ship a safe client patch to strip those fields if needed.
[06:43] Priya Shah: One more operational question — when you say 'protected quota' is that per node or global? We run a sharded KV across nodes.
[06:52] Maya Singh: It's a global policy enforced by the orchestration layer, but the runtime keeps local heuristics. For sharded setups we replicate some metadata so protected keys get preferential placement. We'll include architecture notes in the doc.
[07:05] Elena Gomez: For the SOC/ISO artifacts, please include an explicit statement on who can access raw logs and whether Redwood personnel can decrypt with a customer-specific key or not.
[07:15] Jordan Park: Understood — we'll clarify that in the compliance pack. For private/dedicated deployments customers can bring their own KMS so Redwood never has plaintext access.
[07:25] Alex Romero: Back to cost/latency tradeoffs — can you show a couple of concrete configurations? Like config A: no prefetch, LRU-only; config B: protected quota + shadow canonicalization; config C: B + aggressive prefetch + temporary reserved capacity.
[07:39] Maya Singh: Yes — we'll produce a 3-line comparison table with expected KV hit, p50/p95, and estimated incremental infra cost.
[07:46] Jordan Park: We'll attach that to the benchmark spreadsheet.
[07:50] [Interrupt — brief side chat about calendar invites; 2 attendees muted briefly]
[08:05] Alex Romero: Quick question on rollout — if we enable canonicalization server-side, how do we do canary?
[08:12] Maya Singh: Canary as follows: enable for 10% of sessions with shadow on for 100%, collect collision rate and quality drift using the hashed sidecar, then expand to 50%, then to 100 if safe. We can also do model-level canary: route model variant with canonicalization to a small subset.
[08:30] Priya Shah: That works.
[08:32] Jordan Park: Anything else on the engineering side before we go to security?
[08:36] Mark Li: No, just one ask: please include raw sim logs or a link to them so our SREs can run independent checks.
[08:44] Maya Singh: We'll provide logs (redacted) and a readme on how to replay. Link will be in the follow-up.
[08:51] Elena Gomez: On the redaction: we need to ensure PII is removed; provide a schema of fields stored. Also show proof of encryption at rest and in transit.
[09:00] Jordan Park: Will do. We'll include the logs schema and the KMS encryption assertion.
[09:06] Alex Romero: Ok I'm going to show two small traces to highlight the issue. (Screen share audio — transcription noisy)
[09:12] Alex Romero: Trace one — session A shows repeated prefix P1 but with appended telemetry ts=… so it missed cache. Trace two — session B had stable prefix and hit.
[09:22] Maya Singh: The key takeaways — small normalization change recovers a lot of hit-rate for P1 class; for the churn class, protected quota plus modest reserved capacity avoids p95 spikes.
[09:35] Jordan Park: Good. Let's capture risk areas: 1) false positive collisions from canonicalization (quality risk), 2) memory bloat if protected quota mis-sized, 3) ops complexity in sharded KV. We'll make rollback safe.
[09:50] Priya Shah: On the staging plan — we'll need a rollout runbook and a kill-switch that disables protected quota quickly.
[09:58] Maya Singh: Rollback is simple — flip the policy flag in the control plane; we'll provide runbook steps and playbook.
[10:06] Mark Li: Great. Next — timeline: can we get the eviction sim results by next Monday?
[10:11] Jordan Park: That's July 6th; Maya aiming for July 6th. But we also need prompt set earlier — July 3rd — can Cedar commit to that?
[10:19] Alex Romero: Yes we'll get the top-500 prompts to you by Friday (July 3rd).
[10:24] Elena Gomez: Also will review compliance pack and follow up with comments by July 7th.
[10:30] Jordan Park: Perfect. Any competitor concerns? Alex mentioned VendorX had an in-house hybrid cache, but none of you are tied to them so far?
[10:39] Alex Romero: We've done a short eval of VendorX; their monitoring was ok but they lacked prefetch sophistication.
[10:45] Maya Singh: Anthropic came up in a couple of threads — they have a different serving model, but similar tradeoffs on batching. Not a blocker though.
[10:53] Jordan Park: Ok wrapping up — recap of the next steps: Jordan sends cost/batching projection and benchmark sheet; Maya runs eviction sim with shadow canonicalization and shares logs + top-200 prefix CSV; Cedar shares top-500 prompts; Elena to review compliance pack. Schedule follow-up deep-dive on 2026-07-08 10:00 PT.
[11:13] Priya Shah: All right thanks everyone.
[11:15] Mark Li: Thanks.
[11:16] Alex Romero: Thanks team.
[11:17] Jordan Park: Thanks — meeting adjourned.
[11:20] [Post-meeting notes pasted in chat: Link to drive/cedar/pilot/benchmark-2026-06-30.xlsx, compliance-pack link: drive/cedar/compliance/pack-2026-06.pdf]
